description: Touch the highest point you can on a wall, then jump and touch again. The gap between those marks is the truth about your Achilles stiffness, the spring setting that decides how much of your strength becomes air. Measure it, understand the spring, and learn why lean legs were built for this.

scenes.narration: Stand sideways next to a wall, reach up as high as you can with the near hand, and mark that point: a piece of tape, a chalked fingertip, a friend's finger held at the spot. Now step back, sink, swing your arms and jump, touching the wall at the very top of your flight. Mark that too. The distance between the two marks, in centimeters, is your vertical jump, and it is your number today. Three jumps, best gap counts, no running start, this is a standing jump. Keep the number. Here is the truth this episode is named for: your jump height is only partly about how strong your legs are. The dip before the jump loads a spring, the spring fires, and how much of your strength survives the transfer into air depends on the stiffness of one tendon you have already met this season. Two guys with identical squats can own jumps fifteen centimeters apart, and the difference is coiled at the back of the ankle. By the end, you will know how stiff your spring is, and how much height it is hiding.

scenes.label: WHERE STRENGTH BECOMES AIR
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Forty centimeters is where a recreational jump becomes an athletic one. Under thirty, your spring is absorbing force it should be returning, and the good news hidden in that sentence is that springs are trainable. Thirty to forty, the system works; technique and tendon work will walk you upward month by month. Over fifty-five, you own the kind of bounce that turns heads in gyms, because vertical jump is the most honest power-to-weight exam in sport. Understand the grading: this number multiplies two things, the force your legs can produce and the percentage of it your spring returns instead of leaking. Most guys train only the first factor for years and wonder why the wall stops moving. Your number today grades the product, and this episode is about the forgotten second factor.
scenes.sub: under 30 cm: a leaking spring - over 55 cm: elite bodyweight bounce

lines: The dip loads the Achilles like a spring.
Stiffer springs return more of the load.
beats.title: THE STRETCH-SHORTENING CYCLE

scenes.narration: Watch the dip in slow motion, because the secret lives there. As you sink, your Achilles tendon stretches under the load of your descending body, storing elastic energy exactly like the pogo spring from the bounce test. Then you reverse direction, and if the reversal is quick, the tendon recoils and adds its stored energy to your muscles' push, free height paid for by physics. Scientists call this the stretch-shortening cycle, and it has a strict rule: the energy leaks away as heat if you pause at the bottom. A slow, deep, paused jump is a muscle jump. A quick, snappy dip is a spring jump, and spring jumps are higher. Stiffness decides the exchange rate. A stiffer Achilles stretches less, stores the energy in a tighter coil, and returns it faster and fuller. A soft one stretches long, returns late, and pays you back in a smaller currency. Your gap on the wall is the exchange rate, printed in centimeters.

Testing keeps confirming the same uncomfortable story for strength-only training. When researchers compare jumpers with similar leg strength, the ones with stiffer Achilles tendons jump higher, transfer force faster, and waste less of the dip. And when training studies add tendon-focused work, heavy slow calf loading and low-level plyometrics, jump height climbs even when muscle size barely changes, because the spring's exchange rate improved. There is a second lab lesson in your number: jump height tracks the health of the whole spring system so well that sports scientists use it as a daily readiness check. A jump that suddenly drops several centimeters is the nervous system and tendons filing a fatigue report. Your wall is not just a test. Used weekly, it is a dashboard, and the number you wrote down today is its first reading.

beats.label: IS THE SWEET SPOT FOR MOST

beats.text: FAST DOWN, NO PAUSE, FULL SWING

scenes.narration: The deep dive is the dip itself, because technique is where your spring gets its orders. Three settings decide the transfer. Depth: a quarter dip for most jumpers; sink to a half squat and the spring unloads and the muscles must rebuild force from zero. Speed: the dip should be fast, almost reckless, because the stretch reflex and the tendon's recoil both reward a quick load. Timing: no pause, ever; the instant you reach the bottom you are already leaving, and the arms swing through the same instant to add their percentage. Film one jump from the side on your retest and watch the bottom position. If there is a visible sit at the bottom of your dip, you are watching centimeters evaporate. The spring was loaded and then politely unloaded before it could fire.

Your advantage on the wall is the season's recurring gift in its purest form. The spring must lift your entire body against gravity, so every centimeter of height is bought with force divided by mass. A heavier jumper needs a dramatically stronger spring just to match your gap, because his spring spends its first wages lifting the extra cargo before buying a single centimeter. This is why jumping has always been a lean athlete's showcase, from high jumpers to dunk artists: the exam grades the ratio, and your ratio starts ahead. Add the fact that your spring can be trained with more frequent, cheaper practice jumps, since each landing bills your joints less, and the conclusion is unavoidable. Of all the numbers in this season, this is the one your body was most specifically built to raise.

Now we jump together. Four rounds: twenty seconds of countermovement jumps, fast dip, no pause, full arm swing, soft landing, reset tall between reps. Rest forty seconds between rounds. Every jump should chase your best gap, never a tired one.

beats.text: JUMP TWICE A WEEK, ALWAYS FRESH
HEAVY CALF WORK STIFFENS THE SPRING
NO MAX JUMPS ON TIRED LEGS

scenes.narration: Your protocol for the next thirty days. Jump twice a week, always fresh: five sets of three maximum countermovement jumps, full recovery, full swing, and the set ends the moment your height visibly drops, because tired jumping teaches the spring to be slow. Twice a week, stiffen the spring itself with heavy slow calf raises, three seconds up and three seconds down, progressing to single leg, the exact load profile tendons answer to. Keep the bounce work from earlier this season in once a week, short and crisp, to keep contact times quick. And use the wall as your dashboard: one honest jump check each week, same time of day, and let the number tell you whether the system is building or begging for rest. Springs are trained with load and respected with rest. Both halves are the program.

So, your gap. Under thirty centimeters: your spring is leaking, and leaks are the best diagnosis in jumping, because the strength is probably already there waiting for a better exchange rate. Thirty to forty: a working spring with technique money still on the table; the dip fixes alone can buy you centimeters this month. Forty to fifty-five: genuinely athletic bounce, the spring and the strength are shaking hands. Over fifty-five: elite bodyweight air, protect the tendon that built it and keep the dashboard running. Put your centimeters in the comments, just the number, and retest in thirty days: same wall, same marks, same three honest jumps. The wall does not negotiate. It just keeps score, and your score is about to move.

Thirty days from now, same wall, same two marks, bring me a bigger gap and we will talk about what it does to your broad jump and your sprint. Subscribe, and keep your number safe until then. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
